description: We are Suki to Sukses, a two-person team dedicated to bringing space science to life through interactive storytelling and custom digital illustration. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are tackling the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by building an engaging web-based storybook that introduces young space enthusiasts to NASA's legacy hardware on the Moon and Mars.
summary: What happens to the spacecraft humanity leaves behind after a mission ends? Created for the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge, Echoes of the Cosmos: An Interstellar Journey answers that question for young minds through an interactive, voice-narrated web storybook. Guiding curious fox Emi and gentle otter Otty across four chapters, children meet Flik (the Apollo 11 Lunar Flag Assembly) on the Moon and Oppy (NASA’s Opportunity Mars Rover) at Meridiani Planum. Through synced read-along narration, expandable NASA Fact Boxes, hands-on scene activities, and a three-question quiz, our storybook turns technical mission archives into an approachable adventure that sparks lasting STEM curiosity.
details:
About the Storybook

Echoes of the Cosmos: An Interstellar Journey transforms retired lunar and Martian hardware into a 22-screen interactive, voice-narrated picture book for young learners. Following Emi the fox and Otty the otter across four chapters, children experience:

- Chapter 1: Journey to the Moon (Blasting off into microgravity toward our silver Moon.)

- Chapter 2: The Footprint on the Moon (Discovering the historic Apollo 11 landing site at Tranquility Base and meeting Flik, the Lunar Flag Assembly.)

- Chapter 3: The Resilient Rover on Mars (Landing on the red plains of Meridiani Planum to meet Oppy, NASA's Opportunity Mars Exploration Rover.)

- Chapter 4: A New Horizon (Honoring historic exploration plaques, looking forward to future missions, and completing a three-question explorer quiz.)

Benefits, Creativity & Intended Impact

Instead of a text-heavy encyclopedia or timeline, personifying real NASA artifacts helps children connect emotionally with space engineering, making planetary science fun and accessible for families, classrooms, and early readers without accounts or paid software. Our intended impact is to spark early STEM curiosity and inspire the next generation to appreciate retired spacecraft as lasting milestones of human teamwork and discovery.

Key Features & Factors Considered

- Voice & Read-Along Highlighting: Browser-native Web Speech API gives each character a distinct voice with adjustable reading speed (0.85x, 1.0x, 1.15x) and synced word highlighting, paired with synthesized Web Audio chimes.

- Hands-On Space Discovery: Readers float zero-gravity items in Chapter 1, inspect Flik's horizontal crossbar in Chapter 2, brush Martian dust off Oppy's solar panels in Chapter 3, and open four expandable NASA Fact Boxes (including Historic Exploration Plaques in Chapter 4).

- Child Safety, Accessibility & Accuracy: Built for desktop and mobile (portrait and landscape, keyboard and touch swipe) with localStorage progress saving, zero logins, zero personal data collected, and every historical fact verified against official NASA archives.

How We Built It

- Web & Browser Stack: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Web Speech API, Web Audio API, and localStorage

- Tooling & Hosting: Node.js, Vite, TypeScript, Google Fonts (Fredoka and Nunito), and Vercel

- Official NASA Sources: NASA Solar System Exploration, the Apollo 11 Mission Archive, and the Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity Archive

- AI Assistance Disclosure: Google AI Studio (Gemini) assisted with prototyping, responsive debugging, documentation/presentation drafting, and original fictional illustrations (with no NASA logos or agency branding generated or altered).
